rate.text: One large nationwide study, linked to death records. It didn't account for diet, exercise or income, but those are unlikely to explain a death rate three times as high. The figures on stopping are rougher.
rate.reason: 'A threefold gap' has nothing to point to in the short (years, survival out of 100), and 'threefold' is harder to read. Same reasons kept.

rate.text: One big US government report that sums up other studies and doesn't say how it found them. For nicotine on its own, it leans mostly on animal studies and other products, with few studies of people using nicotine alone.
rate.reason: 'Not on people using nicotine alone' is too absolute: the indirectness note lists trials of medicines, and the reasoning says 'mostly'.

rate.text: Trials where chance decided who got nicotine, but they recorded side effects differently, and only 15 of 136 counted chest pain or a pounding heart, with fairly few cases. Serious problems were too rare to judge.
rate.reason: The rating is for the chest pain finding; its own imprecision reason (about 200 cases) was missing. The serious-event figures carry separate, lower ratings.

rate.text: Many trials where chance decided who got a vape. The review rates the evidence strong, but we rate it moderate: results varied between trials, and some small trials that found nothing may be unpublished.
rate.reason: Uses the site's word for the top level ('strong', as in the evidence bars and the other rate lines) instead of the review's 'high'.

item.statement: Quitting smoking between 55 and 64 is too late to make any difference.
item.why: In a big US study, people who stopped at 55 to 64 gained roughly 4 years compared with people who kept smoking. That's a group average.

quiz.reason: 'After 55' takes in ages the lines don't cover; the figure is for stopping at 55 to 64.

item.statement: Quitting smoking around 40 wipes out all the extra risk of dying early.
item.why: In a big US study, people who stopped around 40 still died at 1.2 times the rate of people who never smoked, against 3 times for those who kept smoking.

quiz.reason: 'By 40' takes in quitting at 25 or 30, which the lines don't measure for this; the lines and the why say 'around 40'.

item.statement: Swedish snus has been shown to raise the risk of mouth cancer.
item.why: In an independent review, mouth cancer showed no clear difference between men who used snus and men who used no tobacco. A world cancer agency rates smokeless tobacco as a whole as causing cancer, without rating snus on its own.

quiz.reason: The why's second sentence named a 'verdict' without saying what it is; it now says it, from how point 4.

item.statement: The label on nicotine pouches always tells you how strong they are.
item.why: In a German lab's test of 44 nicotine pouch products bought in 2021, only 15 printed the nicotine in milligrams, and 4 gave no sign of strength at all.

quiz.reason: The lab tested 44 products, not 44 pouches; labels belong to products (how point 1).

item.statement: A nicotine patch plus gum or similar helped more people quit than one form alone.
item.why: In 16 trials, about 17 in 100 quit for 6 months or more with both, against 14 in 100 with one kind. The gain is small.

quiz.reason: Fix: the trials paired a patch with any quick form; the lines say 'gum or similar', the item said only gum. Advice risk: trial result naming products; could read as advice to combine a patch with gum.

item.statement: In trials, nicotine vapes helped more people quit smoking than patches or gum.
item.why: In 11 trials, about 4 more people in 100 quit for 6 months or more with a vape than with patches or gum. In most trials that checked, more people kept vaping, and effects over years aren't known.

quiz.reason: Fix: 'More people kept vaping' was flat and had no comparison; the But says 'in most trials that checked'. Advice risk: trial result naming a product; could read as advice to use a vape rather than patches to quit.

item.statement: Simply advising people who smoke to vape has been shown to help them quit.
item.why: In 2 trials, advice to vape without giving a vape made no clear difference. Being given one did better than counselling alone or nothing, but those trials couldn't hide who got a vape.

quiz.reason: Fix: 'no clear difference' supports 'not shown to help', not 'doesn't help'; the why now says what being given a vape beat. Advice risk: the why says being given a vape did better; could read as advice to get one.

how: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report says burned tobacco, like cigarettes, causes by far most of tobacco's death and disease in the US. That's about products. It doesn't split the harm between nicotine and the rest of the smoke.

For nicotine alone, it found enough evidence that it can poison in high enough amounts. It also judged that nicotine harms an unborn baby's growing brain and adds to early births and stillbirths. The brain finding comes from lab studies, the pregnancy one mostly from smokeless tobacco and patch trials.

For teenagers' brains, it called the evidence suggestive but not enough. For cancer, it was too thin to say either way. It made no ruling on the heart, but calls it likely that nicotine adds somewhat to heart risk in people who smoke.

It says nicotine is the main thing in tobacco that hooks people, but nicotine medicines carry a low risk of that. Nicotine gave a small boost to thinking in adults who smoke while in withdrawal, and in some who don't smoke. Authors paid by industry reported almost only good effects on thinking.

lines.reason: How point 4 only: keeps 'in withdrawal' for people who smoke, as the statement does (a boost then may be relief of withdrawal); 'tobacco firms' becomes 'industry', since the statement names no industry. Same number and order of points.
Note for editors, not a fix: the magnitude field gives 1.46 after extra adjustment for alcohol, education and activity (six cohorts). The But and how point 2 stress drinking but leave this out.
Advice risk: how point 4's 'may be less harmful than tobacco' (the review authors' view) could read as a nudge to switch.
Advice risk: trial result naming products; 'a patch plus gum or similar did a little better' could read as advice to combine.
Advice risk: how point 3, one patch trial in heart disease finding no more serious problems, could read as safety reassurance.

how: A Cochrane review, updated to January 2026, pooled 11 trials with 4,114 adults who smoked; most trials supplied the vape. If 6 in 100 quit with patches or gum, as the review assumes, about 10 in 100 would quit with a nicotine vape.
Against a vape without nicotine, a nicotine vape helped about 2 more in 100 quit, in 7 trials.

What people used afterwards is less certain. In the vape groups, more people were vaping without smoking, and fewer had stopped both smoking and vaping. How long people kept vaping varied too much between trials to combine.
All trials were in adults, with regulated vapes. The results held without the one trial paid for by industry in each comparison, and without the weakest trials.

lines.reason: How point 3: 'fewer were using neither' is hard to read; it now says 'fewer had stopped both smoking and vaping'. Same number and order of points. Advice risk: trial result naming a product; vapes beat patches or gum, which could read as advice to vape to quit.
Advice risk: trial result naming a product; 'when given a vape' more people quit, which could read as advice to vape.
